claim: IMEF-systems are found in Firmicute genomes.
source: IMEF-systems are found in Firmicute genomes and their operon organization indicates a function in dynamic iron storage.
evidence: Stated directly in the text as a result of computational analysis.

claim: The IMEF operon organization indicates a function in dynamic iron storage.
source: IMEF-systems are found in Firmicute genomes and their operon organization indicates a function in dynamic iron storage.
evidence: Based on inference from operon organization analysis.

claim: 71 IMEF operons were identified in a range of Firmicutes including Quasibacillus thermotolerans.
source: To investigate the distribution of IMEF-systems in microbes, we carried out BLASTp searches using IMEF cargo proteins as queries and identified 71 operons in a range of Firmicutes including Qs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: Direct result from BLASTp searches and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1a.

claim: The core IMEF operon consists of the encapsulin capsid protein and the IMEF cargo protein.
source: The core operon consists of the encapsulin capsid protein and the IMEF cargo protein with 70% of operons also encoding a 2Fe-2S ferredoxin homologous to bacterioferritin-associated ferredoxins (Bfd).
evidence: Direct observation from operon analysis.

claim: 70% of IMEF operons encode a 2Fe-2S ferredoxin homologous to bacterioferritin-associated ferredoxins (Bfd).
source: The core operon consists of the encapsulin capsid protein and the IMEF cargo protein with 70% of operons also encoding a 2Fe-2S ferredoxin homologous to bacterioferritin-associated ferredoxins (Bfd).
evidence: Quantitative result from operon analysis.

claim: Bfd proteins are involved in the mobilization of iron under iron-limited conditions.
source: Bfd proteins are involved in the mobilization of iron under iron-limited conditions (Yao et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yao et al., 2012.

claim: 31% of IMEF operons are associated with proteins similar to ferrochelatases.
source: In addition, 31% of operons are associated with proteins similar to ferrochelatases involved in catalyzing the insertion of ferrous iron into protoporphyrins (Dailey et al., 2000).
evidence: Quantitative result from operon analysis.

claim: Ferrochelatases are involved in catalyzing the insertion of ferrous iron into protoporphyrins.
source: In addition, 31% of operons are associated with proteins similar to ferrochelatases involved in catalyzing the insertion of ferrous iron into protoporphyrins (Dailey et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dailey et al., 2000.

claim: The majority of IMEF-encoding genomes do not contain any ferritin or bacterioferritin genes.
source: The majority of IMEF-encoding genomes do not contain any ferritin or bacterioferritin genes (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Result from genome analysis shown in Supplementary file 1.

claim: Most IMEF genomes contain Dps-encoding genes.
source: Most IMEF genomes do however contain Dps-encoding genes.
evidence: Result from genome analysis.

claim: The structure of the Qs IMEF encapsulin shell was determined at an overall resolution of 3.85 Å.
source: Through single-particle cryo-EM analysis, we determined the structure of the Qs IMEF encapsulin shell at an overall resolution of 3.85 Å (Figure 1—figure supplement 2a and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Direct result from cryo-EM analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2a and Supplementary file 2.

claim: The IMEF encapsulin self-assembles into a 240-subunit icosahedral compartment with a diameter of 42 nm.
source: The IMEF encapsulin self-assembles into a 240-subunit icosahedral compartment with a diameter of 42 nm (Figure 1b and Figure 1—figure supplement 2a–d).
evidence: Direct observation from cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 1b and Figure 1—figure supplement 2a–d.

claim: The IMEF compartment possesses a triangulation number of T = 4.
source: The IMEF compartment is substantially larger than previously reported encapsulins and possesses a triangulation number of T = 4 instead of T = 1 (60 subunits, 24 nm) or T = 3 (180 subunits, 32 nm) and represents the largest encapsulin compartment reported to date (Figure 1—figure supplement 2e).
evidence: Direct observation from structural analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2e.

claim: The IMEF T = 4 encapsulin represents the largest encapsulin compartment reported to date.
source: The IMEF compartment is substantially larger than previously reported encapsulins and possesses a triangulation number of T = 4 instead of T = 1 (60 subunits, 24 nm) or T = 3 (180 subunits, 32 nm) and represents the largest encapsulin compartment reported to date (Figure 1—figure supplement 2e).
evidence: Comparative statement based on structural data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2e.

claim: The T = 4 shell is composed of 12 pentameric and 30 hexameric capsomers.
source: The shell is composed of 12 pentameric and 30 hexameric capsomers occupying icosahedral vertices and faces, respectively.
evidence: Direct observation from structural analysis.

claim: T = 1 encapsulins consist of only 12 pentameric capsomers.
source: In contrast, T = 1 encapsulins consist of only 12 pentameric capsomers while the T = 3 encapsulin shell is made up of 12 pentameric and 20 hexameric capsomers.
evidence: Comparative structural information based on known encapsulin structures.

claim: The T = 3 encapsulin shell is made up of 12 pentameric and 20 hexameric capsomers.
source: In contrast, T = 1 encapsulins consist of only 12 pentameric capsomers while the T = 3 encapsulin shell is made up of 12 pentameric and 20 hexameric capsomers.
evidence: Comparative structural information based on known encapsulin structures.

claim: The T = 4 IMEF-system possesses an internal volume 530% larger than that of T = 1 encapsulins.
source: The T = 4 IMEF-system consequently possesses an internal volume 530% and 220% larger than that of T = 1 and T = 3 encapsulins, respectively.
evidence: Calculated from structural dimensions.

claim: The T = 4 IMEF-system possesses an internal volume 220% larger than that of T = 3 encapsulins.
source: The T = 4 IMEF-system consequently possesses an internal volume 530% and 220% larger than that of T = 1 and T = 3 encapsulins, respectively.
evidence: Calculated from structural dimensions.

claim: The icosahedral asymmetric unit consists of one pentameric and three hexameric monomers.
source: The icosahedral asymmetric unit consists of one pentameric and three hexameric monomers (Figure 1b and Figure 1—figure supplement 2c).
evidence: Direct observation from structural analysis shown in Figure 1b and Figure 1—figure supplement 2c.

claim: Symmetrically arranged lower resolution density (ca. 10 Å) representing the IMEF cargo is visible in the compartment interior.
source: Symmetrically arranged lower resolution density (ca. 10 Å) representing the IMEF cargo is visible in the compartment interior (Figure 1b and Figure 1—figure supplement 2d).
evidence: Direct observation from cryo-EM map shown in Figure 1b and Figure 1—figure supplement 2d.

claim: 42 distinct cargo densities, one for each capsomer of the T = 4 structure, can be observed.
source: 42 distinct densities, one for each capsomer of the T = 4 structure, can be observed.
evidence: Direct observation from cryo-EM analysis.

claim: The distance between the shell and cargo densities is 4.5 nm.
source: The distance between the shell and cargo densities is 4.5 nm which can be bridged by the 37 amino acid linker.
evidence: Measured from cryo-EM structure.

claim: The 37 amino acid linker can bridge the 4.5 nm distance between shell and cargo densities.
source: The distance between the shell and cargo densities is 4.5 nm which can be bridged by the 37 amino acid linker.
evidence: Inference based on structural measurements and linker length.

claim: The four capsid proteins of the asymmetric unit adopt different conformations with significant differences found in the E-loop and A-domain.
source: The four capsid proteins of the asymmetric unit adopt different conformations with significant differences found in the E-loop and A-domain (Figure 1c).
evidence: Direct observation from structural analysis shown in Figure 1c.

claim: E-loops are located at capsomer interfaces and their relative orientation plays a key role in determining the overall topology and triangulation number of encapsulin compartments.
source: E-loops are located at capsomer interfaces and their relative orientation plays a key role in determining the overall topology and triangulation number of encapsulin compartments as evidenced by comparison of the IMEF T = 4 monomer with T = 1 (Thermotoga maritima), T = 3 (Pyrococcus furiosus) and T = 7 (HK97 phage) capsid proteins (Figure 1c).
evidence: Inference from comparative structural analysis shown in Figure 1c.

claim: A-domain loops form compartment pores and are likely adapted to optimize the particular function of a given encapsulin.
source: A-domain loops form compartment pores and are likely adapted to optimize the particular function of a given encapsulin, for example ROS detoxification or iron mineralization.
evidence: Inference from structural observations and functional considerations.

claim: E-loops and A-domain loops represent the most flexible parts of the shell.
source: In addition, local resolution maps indicate that E-loops and A-domain loops represent the most flexible parts of the shell which suggests a certain structural flexibility of the pores formed by A-domain loops (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Direct observation from local resolution maps shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: The IMEF encapsulin shell contains negatively charged pores at the 3- and 5-fold symmetry axes.
source: The IMEF encapsulin shell contains negatively charged pores at the 3- and 5-fold symmetry axes.
evidence: Direct observation from structural analysis.

claim: All pores in the IMEF-system are negatively charged on both the exterior and interior surface due to the presence of conserved aspartate, glutamate and asparagine residues.
source: All pores in the IMEF-system are negatively charged on both the exterior and interior surface due to the presence of conserved aspartate, glutamate and asparagine residues (Figure 2a,b, Figure 2—figure supplement 1b and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Direct observation from structural analysis shown in Figure 2a,b, Figure 2—figure supplement 1b and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Negatively charged pores in ferritin systems guide positively charged iron to the ferritin interior.
source: This is similar to the negatively charged pores in ferritin systems that guide positively charged iron to the ferritin interior (Arosio et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Arosio et al., 2017.

claim: In no other encapsulin system are all pores negatively charged.
source: In no other encapsulin system are all pores negatively charged indicating that pores in the IMEF-system are optimized for attracting and channeling positively charged ions.
evidence: Comparative observation from structural analysis.

claim: Pores in the IMEF-system are optimized for attracting and channeling positively charged ions.
source: In no other encapsulin system are all pores negatively charged indicating that pores in the IMEF-system are optimized for attracting and channeling positively charged ions.
evidence: Inference from structural observations.

claim: The 2-fold pores observed at the interface of two capsomers in T = 1 and T = 3 encapsulins are not present in the IMEF-system.
source: The 2-fold pores observed at the interface of two capsomers in T = 1 and T = 3 encapsulins are not present in the IMEF-system (Nichols et al., 2017).
evidence: Comparative structural observation supported by citation to Nichols et al., 2017.

claim: The 3-fold pore forms the largest channel to the IMEF compartment interior and is 7.2 Å wide at its narrowest point.
source: The 3-fold pore forms the largest channel to the IMEF compartment interior and is 7.2 Å wide at its narrowest point, substantially larger than previously reported encapsulin pores.
evidence: Measured from structural analysis.

claim: The 3-fold pore is substantially larger than previously reported encapsulin pores.
source: The 3-fold pore forms the largest channel to the IMEF compartment interior and is 7.2 Å wide at its narrowest point, substantially larger than previously reported encapsulin pores.
evidence: Comparative structural observation.

claim: Extra cryo-EM density is observed at the center of both the 3-fold and 5-fold pores.
source: Extra cryo-EM density is observed at the center of both the 3-fold and 5-fold pores.
evidence: Direct observation from cryo-EM map.

claim: The extra density at pore centers could represent bound ions (e.g. Fe2+/3+) or water molecules.
source: This could be a result of averaging accentuating noise on symmetry axes or potentially represent bound ions (e.g. Fe2+/3+) or even water molecules.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of cryo-EM density.

claim: The conformation of two asparagine side chains prevents the formation of a 2-fold opening in the T = 4 shell leading to a closed pore.
source: The 2-fold symmetry axes at the center of hexameric capsomers also represent potential channels, as observed in T = 3 systems (Nichols et al., 2017), but the conformation of two asparagine side chains prevents the formation of a 2-fold opening in the T = 4 shell leading to a closed pore (Figure 2c).
evidence: Direct observation from structural analysis shown in Figure 2c, with citation to Nichols et al., 2017.

claim: The flexibility observed for loops around the 2- and 5-fold symmetry axes could indicate the presence of gated pores in encapsulins.
source: This observation combined with the flexibility observed for loops around the 2- and 5-fold symmetry axes in local resolution maps (Figure 1—figure supplement 4) could indicate the presence of gated pores in encapsulins that may regulate ion flux to the compartment interior, similar to some ferritins (Theil et al., 2008).
evidence: Inference from structural observations and comparison to ferritins, supported by citation to Theil et al., 2008.

claim: Gated pores may regulate ion flux to the compartment interior, similar to some ferritins.
source: This observation combined with the flexibility observed for loops around the 2- and 5-fold symmetry axes in local resolution maps (Figure 1—figure supplement 4) could indicate the presence of gated pores in encapsulins that may regulate ion flux to the compartment interior, similar to some ferritins (Theil et al., 2008).
evidence: Speculative inference supported by citation to Theil et al., 2008.

claim: The IMEF compartment possesses a non-covalent chainmail topology.
source: The IMEF compartment possesses a non-covalent chainmail topology and is highly thermostable.
evidence: Direct observation from structural analysis.

claim: E-loops and P-domains of neighboring capsid monomers arrange head to tail to form interlocking concatenated rings resulting in a non-covalent chainmail topology.
source: E-loops and P-domains of neighboring capsid monomers arrange head to tail to form interlocking concatenated rings resulting in a non-covalent chainmail topology (Figure 2d) (Zhang et al., 2013).
evidence: Direct observation from structural analysis shown in Figure 2d, supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2013.

claim: Non-covalent chainmail architecture has only been observed in a number of viral capsids including the HK97 bacteriophage but not in a bacterial system.
source: This architecture has only been observed in a number of viral capsids including the HK97 bacteriophage but not in a bacterial system.
evidence: Comparative statement based on structural knowledge.

claim: In HK97 an isopeptide bond covalently links E-loops and P-domains.
source: In contrast to HK97 where an isopeptide bond covalently links E-loops and P-domains (Duda, 1998), the IMEF encapsulin uses non-covalent interactions.
evidence: Comparative structural information supported by citation to Duda, 1998.

claim: The IMEF encapsulin uses non-covalent interactions instead of isopeptide bonds to link E-loops and P-domains.
source: In contrast to HK97 where an isopeptide bond covalently links E-loops and P-domains (Duda, 1998), the IMEF encapsulin uses non-covalent interactions.
evidence: Direct observation from structural analysis.

claim: At each 3-fold pore, E-loops connect with two neighboring P-domains including the G-loop conserved in T = 4 encapsulins.
source: At each 3-fold pore, E-loops connect with two neighboring P-domains including the G-loop conserved in T = 4 encapsulins and their interfaces contain complementary electrostatic as well as aromatic and potential anion-π interactions (Figure 2e and Figure 2—figure supplement 1c,d) (Philip et al., 2011).
evidence: Direct observation from structural analysis shown in Figure 2e and Figure 2—figure supplement 1c,d, supported by citation to Philip et al., 2011.

claim: The interfaces between E-loops and P-domains contain complementary electrostatic as well as aromatic and potential anion-π interactions.
source: At each 3-fold pore, E-loops connect with two neighboring P-domains including the G-loop conserved in T = 4 encapsulins and their interfaces contain complementary electrostatic as well as aromatic and potential anion-π interactions (Figure 2e and Figure 2—figure supplement 1c,d) (Philip et al., 2011).
evidence: Direct observation from structural analysis shown in Figure 2e and Figure 2—figure supplement 1c,d, supported by citation to Philip et al., 2011.

claim: The IMEF cargo protein shows a linear unfolding curve starting at ca. 40°C and extending to ca. 75°C followed by a hyperbolic increase leading to a midpoint of the thermal unfolding curve of 80.6°C.
source: The IMEF cargo protein shows a linear unfolding curve starting at ca. 40°C and extending to ca. 75°C followed by a hyperbolic increase leading to a midpoint of the thermal unfolding curve of 80.6°C.
evidence: Direct result from differential scanning fluorimetry experiments.

claim: The shell protein is highly thermostable with a melting temperature of 86.6°C.
source: The shell protein is highly thermostable with a melting temperature of 86.6°C, respectively (Figure 2f).
evidence: Direct result from differential scanning fluorimetry shown in Figure 2f.

claim: A stabilizing effect is observed for the cargo-loaded compartment (88.9°C).
source: A stabilizing effect is observed for the cargo-loaded compartment (88.9°C).
evidence: Direct result from differential scanning fluorimetry experiments.

claim: Compartments isolated from high iron conditions show even greater thermal stability (91.8°C).
source: Compartments isolated from high iron conditions show even greater thermal stability (91.8°C) likely due to the internal cavity being stabilized by mineralized material.
evidence: Direct result from differential scanning fluorimetry experiments.

claim: The internal cavity is likely stabilized by mineralized material in high iron conditions.
source: Compartments isolated from high iron conditions show even greater thermal stability (91.8°C) likely due to the internal cavity being stabilized by mineralized material.
evidence: Inference from thermal stability measurements.

claim: The IMEF cargo protein is a member of the Flp superfamily and is most closely related to Dps proteins.
source: Phylogenetic analysis revealed that the IMEF cargo protein is a member of the Flp superfamily and is most closely related to Dps proteins (Figure 3a and Supplementary file 3) but no known ferroxidase motifs could be detected based on the primary sequence alone (Andrews, 2010).
evidence: Result from phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 3a and Supplementary file 3, with citation to Andrews, 2010.

claim: No known ferroxidase motifs could be detected in the IMEF cargo protein based on the primary sequence alone.
source: Phylogenetic analysis revealed that the IMEF cargo protein is a member of the Flp superfamily and is most closely related to Dps proteins (Figure 3a and Supplementary file 3) but no known ferroxidase motifs could be detected based on the primary sequence alone (Andrews, 2010).
evidence: Result from sequence analysis, with citation to Andrews, 2010.

claim: IMEF proteins form a separate clade distinct from other Flp proteins associated with encapsulin systems.
source: IMEF proteins form a separate clade distinct from other Flp proteins associated with encapsulin systems.
evidence: Result from phylogenetic analysis.

claim: All IMEF proteins share a conserved C-terminal TP.
source: All IMEF proteins share a conserved C-terminal TP (Figure 3b).
evidence: Result from sequence analysis shown in Figure 3b.

claim: The x-ray crystal structure of the IMEF cargo was determined to a final resolution of 1.72 Å.
source: We determined the x-ray crystal structure of the IMEF cargo to a final resolution of 1.72 Å (Figure 3c and Supplementary file 4).
evidence: Direct result from x-ray crystallography shown in Figure 3c and Supplementary file 4.

claim: The cargo adopts a four-helix bundle fold characteristic of other members of the Flp superfamily.
source: The cargo adopts a four-helix bundle fold characteristic of other members of the Flp superfamily and forms a dimer with two Fe atoms bound at the subunit interface creating a ferroxidase site based on an alternative ferroxidase sequence motif (Figure 3d, Figure 3—figure supplement 1a,b).
evidence: Direct observation from x-ray structure shown in Figure 3d, Figure 3—figure supplement 1a,b.

claim: The IMEF cargo forms a dimer with two Fe atoms bound at the subunit interface creating a ferroxidase site.
source: The cargo adopts a four-helix bundle fold characteristic of other members of the Flp superfamily and forms a dimer with two Fe atoms bound at the subunit interface creating a ferroxidase site based on an alternative ferroxidase sequence motif (Figure 3d, Figure 3—figure supplement 1a,b).
evidence: Direct observation from x-ray structure shown in Figure 3d, Figure 3—figure supplement 1a,b.

claim: The ferroxidase site is based on an alternative ferroxidase sequence motif.
source: The cargo adopts a four-helix bundle fold characteristic of other members of the Flp superfamily and forms a dimer with two Fe atoms bound at the subunit interface creating a ferroxidase site based on an alternative ferroxidase sequence motif (Figure 3d, Figure 3—figure supplement 1a,b).
evidence: Direct observation from x-ray structure shown in Figure 3d, Figure 3—figure supplement 1a,b.

claim: The combined molecular weight of the fully cargo-loaded IMEF compartment is 9.6 MDa.
source: This leads to a combined molecular weight of the fully cargo-loaded IMEF compartment of 9.6 MDa (42 × cargo dimer [22.6 kDa]+240 × capsid protein, [32.2 kDa]).
evidence: Calculated from structural composition.

claim: A set of conserved residues involved in the formation of the dinuclear ferroxidase center was identified through structure and sequence analysis.
source: Through structure and sequence analysis, we identified a set of conserved residues involved in the formation of the dinuclear ferroxidase center.
evidence: Result from structure and sequence analysis.

claim: The IMEF ferroxidase motif differs from known examples and represents an alternative way of forming an inter-subunit ferroxidase center.
source: This IMEF ferroxidase motif differs from known examples and represents an alternative way of forming an inter-subunit ferroxidase center (Figure 3d).
evidence: Comparative structural analysis shown in Figure 3d.

claim: The C-terminal linker and TP are not resolved in the cargo x-ray structure due to flexibility.
source: Due to flexibility, the C-terminal linker and TP are not resolved in the cargo x-ray structure in accordance with observations from our cryo-EM analysis.
evidence: Direct observation from x-ray crystallography.

claim: Removal of the 13 C-terminal residues results in empty encapsulin shells.
source: Removal of the 13 C-terminal residues results in empty encapsulin shells confirming that the IMEF TP is necessary for cargo encapsulation (Figure 3e).
evidence: Direct experimental result shown in Figure 3e.

claim: The IMEF TP is necessary for cargo encapsulation.
source: Removal of the 13 C-terminal residues results in empty encapsulin shells confirming that the IMEF TP is necessary for cargo encapsulation (Figure 3e).
evidence: Inference from experimental result shown in Figure 3e.

claim: Additional cryo-EM densities around the 2- and 5-fold symmetry axes represent bound TPs anchoring IMEF cargo to the interior surface of the compartment.
source: Through analysis of the T = 4 cryo-EM map, additional densities were identified that could not be explained by the encapsulin capsid protein (Figure 3f). These densities represent bound TPs anchoring IMEF cargo to the interior surface of the compartment.
evidence: Direct observation from cryo-EM analysis shown in Figure 3f.

claim: TP densities can be found at all 240 capsid monomers indicating averaging during cryo-EM reconstruction.
source: Even though only 42 cargo densities are observed, TP densities can be found at all 240 capsid monomers indicating averaging during cryo-EM reconstruction.
evidence: Direct observation from cryo-EM analysis.

claim: Strong TP density is observed for all 180 monomers that are part of 2-fold symmetrical hexameric capsomers.
source: Strong TP density is observed for all 180 monomers that are part of 2-fold symmetrical hexameric capsomers (Figure 3f) while substantially weaker density is found for TPs bound to the 60 pentameric monomers (Figure 3—figure supplement 1c) thus revealing higher occupancy and preferential TP binding around 2-fold symmetry axes which can be explained by different binding site conformations (Figure 3—figure supplement 1c–e) and higher local shell mobility (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Direct observation from cryo-EM analysis shown in Figure 3f.

claim: Substantially weaker TP density is found for TPs bound to the 60 pentameric monomers.
source: Strong TP density is observed for all 180 monomers that are part of 2-fold symmetrical hexameric capsomers (Figure 3f) while substantially weaker density is found for TPs bound to the 60 pentameric monomers (Figure 3—figure supplement 1c) thus revealing higher occupancy and preferential TP binding around 2-fold symmetry axes which can be explained by different binding site conformations (Figure 3—figure supplement 1c–e) and higher local shell mobility (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Direct observation from cryo-EM analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1c.

claim: There is higher occupancy and preferential TP binding around 2-fold symmetry axes.
source: Strong TP density is observed for all 180 monomers that are part of 2-fold symmetrical hexameric capsomers (Figure 3f) while substantially weaker density is found for TPs bound to the 60 pentameric monomers (Figure 3—figure supplement 1c) thus revealing higher occupancy and preferential TP binding around 2-fold symmetry axes which can be explained by different binding site conformations (Figure 3—figure supplement 1c–e) and higher local shell mobility (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Inference from cryo-EM density observations shown in Figure 3f and Figure 3—figure supplement 1c.

claim: Preferential TP binding around 2-fold symmetry axes can be explained by different binding site conformations and higher local shell mobility.
source: Strong TP density is observed for all 180 monomers that are part of 2-fold symmetrical hexameric capsomers (Figure 3f) while substantially weaker density is found for TPs bound to the 60 pentameric monomers (Figure 3—figure supplement 1c) thus revealing higher occupancy and preferential TP binding around 2-fold symmetry axes which can be explained by different binding site conformations (Figure 3—figure supplement 1c–e) and higher local shell mobility (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Inference from structural observations shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1c–e and Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: The main TP binding sites surrounding the 2-fold symmetry axes are formed by conserved residues of the P-domain and N-terminal helix.
source: The main TP binding sites surrounding the 2-fold symmetry axes are formed by conserved residues of the P-domain and N-terminal helix (Figure 2—figure supplement 2) similar to the T. maritima T = 1 encapsulin system (Sutter et al., 2008).
evidence: Direct observation from structural analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2, with citation to Sutter et al., 2008.

claim: The TP binding site is similar to the T. maritima T = 1 encapsulin system.
source: The main TP binding sites surrounding the 2-fold symmetry axes are formed by conserved residues of the P-domain and N-terminal helix (Figure 2—figure supplement 2) similar to the T. maritima T = 1 encapsulin system (Sutter et al., 2008).
evidence: Comparative structural observation supported by citation to Sutter et al., 2008.

claim: No TP binding site has been identified for T = 3 encapsulins yet.
source: No TP binding site has been identified for T = 3 encapsulins yet.
evidence: Statement of current knowledge.

claim: The presence of the N-terminal helix and the resulting binding site seems to generally underpin encapsulins' ability to interact with TPs and encapsulate cargo proteins.
source: The presence of the N-terminal helix and the resulting binding site seems to generally underpin encapsulins' ability to interact with TPs and encapsulate cargo proteins.
evidence: Inference from structural observations.

claim: The TP residues TVGSLIQ were tentatively built and refined into the additional density present at hexameric capsomers producing a model with good geometry.
source: The TP residues TVGSLIQ were tentatively built and refined into the additional density present at hexameric capsomers producing a model with good geometry (Figure 3—figure supplement 1e).
evidence: Result from model building shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1e.

claim: The TP binds to a surface groove based on shape complementarity and two key ionic interactions with highly conserved positively charged residues.
source: The TP binds to a surface groove based on shape complementarity and two key ionic interactions with highly conserved positively charged residues locking the TP in place.
evidence: Direct observation from structural analysis.

claim: Heterologous expression of the IMEF core operon in E. coli leads to in vivo formation of large Fe- and P-rich electron-dense particles.
source: Heterologous expression of the IMEF core operon in E. coli leads to in vivo formation of large Fe- and P-rich electron-dense particles.
evidence: Direct experimental observation.

claim: Thin section negative stain TEM of E. coli cells grown in Fe-rich (4 mM) medium and expressing the Qs IMEF core operon results in the formation of clusters of large intracellular electron-dense particles.
source: Thin section negative stain transmission electron microscopy (TEM) of E. coli cells grown in Fe-rich (4 mM) medium and expressing the Qs IMEF core operon results in the formation of clusters of large intracellular electron-dense particles (Figure 4a and Figure 4—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: Direct experimental observation shown in Figure 4a and Figure 4—figure supplement 1a.

claim: STEM-EDS revealed that electron-dense particles primarily contain uniformly distributed Fe, P and O with an estimated Fe:P ratio near 1.
source: Scanning TEM-energy-dispersive x-ray spectroscopy (EDS) revealed that these particles primarily contain uniformly distributed Fe, P and O with an estimated Fe:P ratio near 1 (Figure 4b).
evidence: Direct experimental result from STEM-EDS shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Selected area electron diffraction (SAED) indicates that the mineralized material is amorphous.
source: Selected area electron diffraction (SAED) further indicates that this mineralized material is amorphous (Figure 4—figure supplement 1b,c), similar to bacterioferritin systems (Andrews et al., 1993).
evidence: Direct experimental result from SAED shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1b,c, with citation to Andrews et al., 1993.

claim: The amorphous cores are similar to bacterioferritin systems.
source: Selected area electron diffraction (SAED) further indicates that this mineralized material is amorphous (Figure 4—figure supplement 1b,c), similar to bacterioferritin systems (Andrews et al., 1993).
evidence: Comparative statement supported by citation to Andrews et al., 1993.

claim: The high P content and amorphous cores described for the IMEF encapsulin are similar to bacterioferritin systems.
source: The high P content and amorphous cores described for the IMEF encapsulin are similar to bacterioferritin systems (Aitken-Rogers et al., 2004; Mann et al., 1986).
evidence: Comparative statement supported by citations to Aitken-Rogers et al., 2004 and Mann et al., 1986.

claim: Amorphous material can be more readily mobilized under iron-limited condition than crystallized iron mineral.
source: It has been hypothesized that amorphous material can be more readily mobilized under iron-limited condition than crystallized iron mineral (Watt et al., 1992; Watt et al., 2010).
evidence: Hypothesis from literature supported by citations to Watt et al., 1992 and Watt et al., 2010.

claim: IMEF encapsulins purified from E. coli grown under high Fe conditions contain electron dense cores visible in unstained samples with an average diameter of 23 nm.
source: IMEF encapsulins purified from E. coli grown under high Fe conditions contain electron dense cores visible in unstained samples with an average diameter of 23 nm (Figure 4c,d and Figure 4—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: Direct experimental observation shown in Figure 4c,d and Figure 4—figure supplement 2a.

claim: The largest observed particles are up to 30 nm in diameter.
source: The largest observed particles are up to 30 nm in diameter.
evidence: Direct experimental observation.

claim: The theoretical size limit imposed by the T = 4 encapsulin protein shell is 36 nm.
source: The theoretical size limit imposed by the T = 4 encapsulin protein shell is 36 nm and particles close to this size are observed in thin-sections of Geobacillus natively encoding the IMEF-system (Figure 4—figure supplement 2b–d).
evidence: Calculated from structural dimensions and observed in Figure 4—figure supplement 2b–d.

claim: Particles close to 36 nm in size are observed in thin-sections of Geobacillus natively encoding the IMEF-system.
source: The theoretical size limit imposed by the T = 4 encapsulin protein shell is 36 nm and particles close to this size are observed in thin-sections of Geobacillus natively encoding the IMEF-system (Figure 4—figure supplement 2b–d).
evidence: Direct experimental observation shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2b–d.

claim: EDS analysis of particles isolated from E. coli indicates a Fe:P ratio of 1:1.1.
source: EDS analysis of particles isolated from E. coli and comparison with standards indicate a very similar elemental composition and elemental distribution as observed for thin section samples with a Fe:P ratio of 1:1.1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 3a).
evidence: Direct experimental result from EDS shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3a.

claim: The highest observed number of stored Fe per particle was 23,293 (23.6 nm).
source: The highest observed number of stored Fe per particle was 23,293 (23.6 nm) (Supplementary file 5).
evidence: Direct experimental result from EELS shown in Supplementary file 5.

claim: Extrapolating to the maximum theoretical particle diameter of 36 nm and the highest density observed (3.40 Fe atoms/nm3) leads to a maximum number of Fe atoms that can be stored by the IMEF-system of around 83,000.
source: Extrapolating to the maximum theoretical particle diameter of 36 nm and the highest density observed (3.40 Fe atoms/nm3) leads to a maximum number of Fe atoms that can be stored by the IMEF-system of around 83,000 (Supplementary file 5).
evidence: Calculated from experimental data shown in Supplementary file 5.

claim: IMEF-systems are able to store substantially more iron than any known ferritin system (2,000–4,000 Fe atoms).
source: Thus, IMEF-systems are able to store substantially more iron than any known ferritin system (2,000–4,000 Fe atoms) (Andrews, 1998; Harrison and Arosio, 1996).
evidence: Comparative statement based on experimental data, supported by citations to Andrews, 1998 and Harrison and Arosio, 1996.

claim: No peroxidase activity could be observed for the IMEF cargo.
source: Due to the IMEF cargo being most closely related to Dps proteins we initially performed peroxidase assays using hydrogen peroxide as the oxidant. However, no peroxidase activity could be observed.
evidence: Direct experimental result from peroxidase assays.

claim: For the IMEF cargo alone, a sigmoidal ferroxidase iron oxidation curve was observed indicative of autocatalytic Fe oxidation taking place at newly formed mineral surfaces.
source: For the IMEF cargo alone, a sigmoidal ferroxidase iron oxidation curve was observed indicative of autocatalytic Fe oxidation taking place at newly formed mineral surfaces (Bou-Abdallah et al., 2005; Sun and Chasteen, 1992).
evidence: Direct experimental result from ferroxidase assays, supported by citations to Bou-Abdallah et al., 2005 and Sun and Chasteen, 1992.

claim: Assaying the IMEF cargo-loaded encapsulin results in a typical hyperbolic enzyme catalysis curve.
source: However, assaying the IMEF cargo-loaded encapsulin results in a typical hyperbolic enzyme catalysis curve.
evidence: Direct experimental result from ferroxidase assays.

claim: The encapsulin shell controls the flux of iron to the inside of the compartment leading to a controlled and low concentration of soluble iron in the encapsulin interior.
source: These observations imply that the encapsulin shell controls the flux of iron to the inside of the compartment leading to a controlled and low concentration of soluble iron in the encapsulin interior.
evidence: Inference from ferroxidase assay results.

claim: The IMEF cargo protein is able to enzymatically oxidize the majority of ferrous iron before uncontrolled autocatalytic mineralization can lead to bulk precipitation of iron.
source: Therefore, the IMEF cargo protein is able to enzymatically oxidize the majority of ferrous iron before uncontrolled autocatalytic mineralization can lead to bulk precipitation of iron which would likely destroy the iron storage function of the IMEF-system (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Inference from ferroxidase assay results shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: The IMEF-system can in principle store more than 20 times more Fe than Ftn or Bfr systems.
source: The IMEF-system can in principle store more than 20 times more Fe than Ftn or Bfr systems.
evidence: Calculated from experimental data.

claim: IMEF encapsulins are two-component systems with the catalytic activity separated from the protein shell.
source: In contrast to ferritin systems, IMEF encapsulins are two-component systems with the catalytic activity separated from the protein shell.
evidence: Direct observation from structural and functional analysis.

claim: The IMEF cargo protein is flexibly tethered and primarily localizes 4.5 nm away from the capsid interior.
source: The IMEF cargo protein is flexibly tethered and primarily localizes 4.5 nm away from the capsid interior.
evidence: Direct observation from cryo-EM structure.

claim: Once iron enters the encapsulin interior via pores, it diffuses to the ferroxidase active site of the IMEF cargo.
source: This suggests that once iron enters the encapsulin interior via pores, it diffuses to the ferroxidase active site of the IMEF cargo, making it necessary to strictly control interior iron concentration to prevent runaway mineralization.
evidence: Inference from structural and functional observations.

claim: It is necessary to strictly control interior iron concentration to prevent runaway mineralization.
source: This suggests that once iron enters the encapsulin interior via pores, it diffuses to the ferroxidase active site of the IMEF cargo, making it necessary to strictly control interior iron concentration to prevent runaway mineralization.
evidence: Inference from structural and functional observations.

claim: In ferritin systems the ferroxidase activity is part of the shell and negatively charged surface patches guide iron from the pores to ferroxidase sites.
source: This is different compared with ferritin systems where the ferroxidase activity is part of the shell and negatively charged surface patches guide iron from the pores to ferroxidase sites.
evidence: Comparative statement based on established knowledge of ferritin systems.

claim: IMEF-systems are confined to spore-forming Firmicutes.
source: It is striking that IMEF-systems are confined to spore-forming Firmicutes.
evidence: Observation from computational analysis.

claim: IMEF-encoding organisms inhabit a broad range of habitats with many of them initially isolated from hot springs or soil.
source: They inhabit a broad range of habitats with many of them initially isolated from hot springs or soil, environments with often limited or fluctuating iron availability (Colombo et al., 2014; Hou et al., 2013; Huang et al., 2013).
evidence: Observation from literature supported by citations to Colombo et al., 2014, Hou et al., 2013, and Huang et al., 2013.

claim: Hot springs and soil are environments with often limited or fluctuating iron availability.
source: They inhabit a broad range of habitats with many of them initially isolated from hot springs or soil, environments with often limited or fluctuating iron availability (Colombo et al., 2014; Hou et al., 2013; Huang et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Colombo et al., 2014, Hou et al., 2013, and Huang et al., 2013.

claim: The ability to store a much larger amount of iron than other microbes might benefit IMEF-encoding organisms in environments with limited or fluctuating iron availability.
source: The ability to store a much larger amount of iron than other microbes might benefit IMEF-encoding organisms in these environments and thereby contribute to their wide geographical distribution (Zeigler, 2014).
evidence: Speculative inference supported by citation to Zeigler, 2014.

claim: The ability to store large amounts of iron might contribute to the wide geographical distribution of IMEF-encoding organisms.
source: The ability to store a much larger amount of iron than other microbes might benefit IMEF-encoding organisms in these environments and thereby contribute to their wide geographical distribution (Zeigler, 2014).
evidence: Speculative inference supported by citation to Zeigler, 2014.

claim: Iron is essential to virtually all organisms on earth.
source: Iron is essential to virtually all organisms on earth.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge.

claim: Iron is needed for a wide variety of catalytic and redox processes ranging from cellular energy production via oxidative phosphorylation to oxygen transport by hemoglobin.
source: It is needed for a wide variety of catalytic and redox processes ranging from cellular energy production via oxidative phosphorylation to oxygen transport by hemoglobin (Sánchez et al., 2017).
evidence: Established scientific knowledge supported by citation to Sánchez et al., 2017.

claim: The same properties that make iron useful for cellular metabolism can result in toxicity under aerobic conditions.
source: However, the same properties that make iron useful for cellular metabolism can result in toxicity under aerobic conditions (Sánchez et al., 2017).
evidence: Established scientific knowledge supported by citation to Sánchez et al., 2017.

claim: Ferrous iron (Fe2+) is easily oxidized to insoluble ferric iron (Fe3+) resulting in the formation of harmful precipitates and reactive oxygen species (ROS) via Fenton chemistry.
source: Ferrous iron (Fe2+) is easily oxidized to insoluble ferric iron (Fe3+) resulting in the formation of harmful precipitates and reactive oxygen species (ROS) via Fenton chemistry (Dixon and Stockwell, 2014).
evidence: Established scientific knowledge supported by citation to Dixon and Stockwell, 2014.

claim: Cells have evolved to cope with iron toxicity problems by strictly controlling the intracellular concentration and reactivity of free iron.
source: Cells have evolved to cope with these problems by strictly controlling the intracellular concentration and reactivity of free iron (Crichton, 2002).
evidence: Established scientific knowledge supported by citation to Crichton, 2002.

claim: Ferritin proteins are used as the main iron storage system by animals, plants and most microbes.
source: Ferritin proteins are used as the main iron storage system by animals, plants and most microbes (Arosio et al., 2017).
evidence: Established scientific knowledge supported by citation to Arosio et al., 2017.

claim: The main ferritin-like proteins involved in iron storage are ferritin (Ftn), bacterioferritin (Bfr) and DNA-binding proteins from starved cells (Dps).
source: The main ferritin-like proteins involved in iron storage are ferritin (Ftn), bacterioferritin (Bfr) and DNA-binding proteins from starved cells (Dps) all able to oxidize Fe2+ to Fe3+ via a ferroxidase activity (Andrews, 2010).
evidence: Established scientific knowledge supported by citation to Andrews, 2010.

claim: Ftn, Bfr and Dps are all able to oxidize Fe2+ to Fe3+ via a ferroxidase activity.
source: The main ferritin-like proteins involved in iron storage are ferritin (Ftn), bacterioferritin (Bfr) and DNA-binding proteins from starved cells (Dps) all able to oxidize Fe2+ to Fe3+ via a ferroxidase activity (Andrews, 2010).
evidence: Established scientific knowledge supported by citation to Andrews, 2010.

claim: Ftn and Bfr are primarily used as a dynamic iron storage.
source: While Ftn and Bfr are primarily used as a dynamic iron storage (Honarmand Ebrahimi et al., 2015), the main function of Dps proteins is to counteract oxidative stress (Chiancone et al., 2004).
evidence: Established scientific knowledge supported by citation to Honarmand Ebrahimi et al., 2015.

claim: The main function of Dps proteins is to counteract oxidative stress.
source: While Ftn and Bfr are primarily used as a dynamic iron storage (Honarmand Ebrahimi et al., 2015), the main function of Dps proteins is to counteract oxidative stress (Chiancone et al., 2004).
evidence: Established scientific knowledge supported by citation to Chiancone et al., 2004.

claim: Ferritins (Ftn and Bfr) assemble into 24 subunit protein compartments up to 12 nm in diameter able to store 2000 to 4,000 Fe atoms in their interior.
source: Ferritins (Ftn and Bfr) assemble into 24 subunit protein compartments up to 12 nm in diameter able to store 2000 to 4,000 Fe atoms in their interior (Andrews, 1998; Harrison and Arosio, 1996).
evidence: Established scientific knowledge supported by citations to Andrews, 1998 and Harrison and Arosio, 1996.

claim: Some organisms do not encode ferritin genes in their genomes and their iron storage systems have remained elusive.
source: However, some organisms do not encode ferritin genes in their genomes and their iron storage systems have remained elusive.
evidence: Statement of knowledge gap.

claim: Encapsulin nanocompartments have been shown to be involved in microbial iron storage and redox metabolism.
source: A newly discovered class of protein organelles called encapsulin nanocompartments have been shown to be involved in microbial iron storage and redox metabolism (Giessen and Silver, 2017; He et al., 2016; McHugh et al., 2014; Sutter et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Giessen and Silver, 2017, He et al., 2016, McHugh et al., 2014, and Sutter et al., 2008.

claim: Previously reported encapsulins share an HK97 phage-like fold.
source: Previously reported encapsulins share an HK97 phage-like fold and self-assemble from a single capsid protein into icosahedral compartments between 24 and 32 nm in diameter with triangulation numbers of T = 1 (60 subunits) and T = 3 (180 subunits), respectively (Akita et al., 2007; McHugh et al., 2014; Sutter et al., 2008).
evidence: Established knowledge supported by citations to Akita et al., 2007, McHugh et al., 2014, and Sutter et al., 2008.

claim: Previously reported encapsulins self-assemble from a single capsid protein into icosahedral compartments between 24 and 32 nm in diameter with triangulation numbers of T = 1 (60 subunits) and T = 3 (180 subunits).
source: Previously reported encapsulins share an HK97 phage-like fold and self-assemble from a single capsid protein into icosahedral compartments between 24 and 32 nm in diameter with triangulation numbers of T = 1 (60 subunits) and T = 3 (180 subunits), respectively (Akita et al., 2007; McHugh et al., 2014; Sutter et al., 2008).
evidence: Established knowledge supported by citations to Akita et al., 2007, McHugh et al., 2014, and Sutter et al., 2008.

claim: The key feature of encapsulins is the ability to specifically encapsulate cargo proteins.
source: Their key feature is the ability to specifically encapsulate cargo proteins (Figure 1a).
evidence: Established knowledge shown in Figure 1a.

claim: Encapsulation is mediated by short C-terminal sequences referred to as targeting peptides (TPs).
source: Encapsulation is mediated by short C-terminal sequences referred to as targeting peptides (TPs) (Sutter et al., 2008; Tamura et al., 2015).
evidence: Established knowledge supported by citations to Sutter et al., 2008 and Tamura et al., 2015.

claim: Genes encoding encapsulin shell proteins and dedicated cargo proteins are organized in co-regulated operons.
source: Genes encoding encapsulin shell proteins and dedicated cargo proteins are organized in co-regulated operons (Giessen and Silver, 2017; Sutter et al., 2008).
evidence: Established knowledge supported by citations to Giessen and Silver, 2017 and Sutter et al., 2008.

claim: Encapsulin operons involved in hydrogen peroxide and nitric oxide detoxification as well as iron mineralization have been reported.
source: So far, operons involved in hydrogen peroxide and nitric oxide detoxification as well as iron mineralization have been reported (Nichols et al., 2017).
evidence: Established knowledge supported by citation to Nichols et al., 2017.

claim: The main cargo protein-types described to date are DyP-type peroxidases, hemerythrins and different classes of ferritin-like proteins.
source: The main cargo protein-types described to date are DyP-type peroxidases, hemerythrins and different classes of ferritin-like proteins (Contreras et al., 2014; Giessen and Silver, 2017; McHugh et al., 2014; Rahmanpour and Bugg, 2013).
evidence: Established knowledge supported by citations to Contreras et al., 2014, Giessen and Silver, 2017, McHugh et al., 2014, and Rahmanpour and Bugg, 2013.

claim: A novel type of encapsulin operon involved in iron metabolism in a range of Firmicutes was identified and termed the Iron-Mineralizing Encapsulin-Associated Firmicute (IMEF)-system.
source: We have identified a novel type of encapsulin operon involved in iron metabolism in a range of Firmicutes we term the Iron-Mineralizing Encapsulin-Associated Firmicute (IMEF)-system (Giessen and Silver, 2017).
evidence: Direct result from computational analysis, supported by citation to Giessen and Silver, 2017.

claim: This compartment has an exceptionally large iron storage capacity storing over 23,000 iron atoms.
source: This compartment has an exceptionally large iron storage capacity storing over 23,000 iron atoms.
evidence: Direct experimental result from EELS.

claim: The IMEF iron storage system is able to store 10 to 20 times more iron than ferritin.
source: Our results reveal a new approach for survival in diverse habitats with limited or fluctuating iron availability via an iron storage system able to store 10 to 20 times more iron than ferritin.
evidence: Calculated from experimental data.
